hook.support: You join a footy club. They hand you a code of conduct to sign. Most people sign it without reading. But it tells you the rules, and what happens if you break them.
hook.core: You join a footy club, a gym or a new job, and someone hands you a code of conduct to sign. Most people sign without reading. But that document says how everyone must behave, how to report problems, and what happens if you break the rules. It might even protect you.
hook.extend: Clubs, workplaces and community groups run on written charters and codes of conduct. They state the group’s values and the behaviour it expects. They explain how to raise concerns and what happens if rules are broken. Read them carefully, and you learn your rights, your duties, and how the group sees itself.

why.support: A code tells you the rules. It also tells you how to get help.
why.core: Codes of conduct are part of joining almost anything: a team, a job, a club, a course. Knowing what they say protects you, and helps you stand up for others.
why.extend: Charters and codes shape behaviour in every group you’ll join. Reading them closely helps you know your duties, use the complaint process, and judge if a group lives up to its own words.

articles.title: What a code of conduct is for

body.support:
Clubs, jobs and schools have rules. They write them in a **code of conduct** or a **charter**.

Most codes have five parts:

1. **Why.** What the group cares about. Like respect and fair play.
2. **Who.** Who must follow it. Players? Parents? Staff?
3. **Do and don’t.** What you **must** do. What is **not OK**.
4. **Report it.** Who to tell if something goes wrong.
5. **What happens.** A warning. A ban. Or being asked to leave.
.
Look for the word **must**. It means you have to.

Read a code before you sign it. It tells you the rules. It also tells you how to get help.
body.core:
Almost every group you join has written rules: a **code of conduct**, a **charter**, or team rules. They’re there to keep people safe and make sure everyone knows what’s expected.

Most codes have five parts:

1. **Why:** the purpose and the **values**, like respect, fair play and safety.
2. **Who:** who the code applies to. At a sports club, that often includes players, coaches, parents and **spectators**.
3. **Do and don’t:** expected behaviour, and what’s not accepted (like abuse, bullying or discrimination).
4. **Report it:** who to tell and how: a coach, a manager, a club welfare officer, an email.
5. **What happens:** the **consequences**, often in steps: a warning, a suspension, a ban.
.
Watch the small words. **Must** and **will** mean it’s compulsory. **Should** is strongly expected. **May** means it’s allowed, or might happen. **Zero tolerance** means it won’t be accepted at all.

Read a code before you sign it. It sets your obligations, but it also protects you, and tells you exactly how to get help.
body.extend:
Charters and codes of conduct are how groups put their values into writing. A **charter** usually states a group’s purpose and commitments. A **code of conduct** sets out the behaviour expected of members and what happens if it isn’t met.

Typical structure:

1. **Purpose and values:** why the code exists and what the group stands for.
2. **Scope:** who it covers. Sports clubs often include spectators and parents, not just players.
3. **Expected and unacceptable behaviour:** often written as lists.
4. **Reporting process:** who to contact, how, and how confidentiality is handled.
5. **Consequences:** usually graduated (warning, suspension, exclusion).
.
The language matters. Modal verbs signal obligation: **must** and **will** are compulsory; **should** is strong expectation; **may** gives permission or possibility. Phrases like **zero tolerance** signal what the group treats as most serious.

Read critically. What does the code’s wording tell you about the group’s values? Does it protect everyone, including those with less power, like junior umpires or new staff? And does the group actually enforce it?

caseStudies.title: The whistle-blowers

body.support:
Without umpires, there is no footy game. But many umpires get abused.

Researchers asked **356** footy umpires about it.

About **half** said people abused them with words at least every couple of games.

About **1 in 5** said they had been pushed, hit or attacked.

Just over half had reported it.

The researchers said clubs must look after umpires. If not, umpires may quit.

That’s one big reason clubs have a **code of conduct**.
body.core:
Without umpires, there’s no game. But many footy umpires cop abuse from players, coaches and the crowd. Lots of them are teenagers.

Researchers from a university in South Australia asked **356** footy umpires about it. The results came out in 2025.

- **49%** said they were abused with words at least every couple of games.
- **21%** said they had been pushed, hit or attacked.
- **53%** had reported at least one incident.
.
The researchers said clubs must keep their umpires. Umpires who feel supported are more likely to stay.

That’s why most clubs have codes of conduct that cover **spectators** and parents, not just players. The codes say how to report abuse, and what happens next.
body.extend:
Community sport needs umpires. Yet many umpires, often teenagers, say they are abused by players, coaches and spectators.

Researchers from the **University of South Australia** surveyed **356** Australian rules football umpires in 2021 and 2022. Their findings came out in 2025.

- **49%** experienced verbal abuse at least every couple of games.
- **21%** reported physical abuse (pushing, hitting or assault).
- **53%** had reported at least one incident.
.
The researchers argued that keeping umpires must come first. Umpires who feel supported are more likely to stay.

Codes of conduct are one response. Many now cover spectators and parents, say how to report abuse, and set penalties that grow. Some sports make clubs responsible for their fans. But a code only works if people know it, report problems, and see it enforced.

model.text:
**Year 11 VM Group Chat: Our Code**

**Why:** This chat is for sharing work info and helping each other. Everyone should feel safe here.

**Who:** Everyone in the chat, including teachers.

**Everyone must:**
- keep posts about school and work
- ask before sharing someone’s photo

**Not OK:** put-downs, spam, or sharing private info. We have zero tolerance for bullying.

**Report it:** message the class rep or tell Ms Lee.

**What happens:** 1st time, a private warning. 2nd time, removed from the chat for a week.
why: It has all five parts, each with a clear heading.
It uses “must” for compulsory rules and “zero tolerance” for the most serious one.
The consequences are clear and get stronger in steps.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 values (purpose); 2 scope (who it covers, including parents and spectators); 3 compulsory behaviour (“must”); 4 unacceptable behaviour, zero tolerance; 5 reporting pathway; 6 graduated consequences.

**Sort:** parent yelling — breaks; coach asking calmly — OK; racist comment — breaks; cheering both teams — OK; online post — breaks; emailing the Welfare Officer — OK.

**Case study:** 49% verbal abuse at least every couple of games, 21% physical abuse, 53% had reported an incident; codes cover parents and spectators because much abuse comes from the crowd; codes work when they’re known, reported and enforced.

realityCheck: **Students may have experienced abuse as players or umpires.** Keep discussion general; follow up privately if someone discloses something serious.
**Group writing can be dominated by one student.** Give roles (scribe, chair, checker) and use the “What I said” question as evidence of each person’s contribution.
**Real codes are often long and legalistic.** For the Level Up, a one-page club code works better than a 40-page policy.
**A class code can become a real class agreement.** If students want to adopt theirs, let them; it gives the task real stakes.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Sport and group chats are topics students have strong views on.
